title: It's a shame
article: A provincial court judge concluded last week Winnipeg police were justified in shooting a Winnipeg man suffering from psychosis when he nearly beheaded another tenant of a community residence in 2007. Judge Lee Ann Martin forces people to read between the lines, however, to figure out what needs to be done to prevent a similar tragedy from occurring.

Judge Martin, asked to review the circumstances of Ahmed Saleh-Azad's death at Madison Memorial Lodge, stuck strictly to decisions by police officers when they responded to a 911 call on that February morning. Her mandate, she said, did not allow her to examine the quality of his supports while at Madison or the death of his victim, Alexander Kolesnyk.

Mr. Saleh-Azad had home care to ensure he was taking his medications, support from a mental health worker and a psychiatrist. After almost two years of living at Madison, he stopped taking his drugs, something no one noticed until a search of his room after the tragedy.

The judge said Mr. Saleh-Azad fell through the cracks, but not how. She said his psychiatrist believed he did not meet the criteria for an involuntary placement for an assessment, but does not elaborate. She recommended that the province look at how it houses and meets the needs of the mentally ill in the community and also review the Mental Health Act's requirements for involuntary placement.

There is much to be improved in housing and community services for the mentally ill. It is a shame the inquest did not examine both - sorting the facts behind the shooting was the easy part. The superficial treatment of the deaths is a disservice to both men and to the mentally ill struggling to live among us.
